title: A Podcast on Reciprocity in the Age of Constant Messaging
script: Host: [thoughtful] Today's guest is a sociologist who studies how constant connectivity has reshaped what we expect from friendship. Welcome, Teguh.
Guest: Thanks for having me. It's a subject I find endlessly fascinating, mostly because everyone assumes being more connected automatically means being closer.
Host: [carefully] And that's not necessarily true, according to your research?
Guest: Not at all. What we've found is that constant low-effort contact, likes, reactions, forwarded posts, can actually substitute for the deeper conversations that used to sustain friendships.
Host: [reflective] So people feel connected without the relationship actually being maintained?
Guest: Precisely. There's an illusion of closeness that comes from seeing someone's updates daily, even if you haven't had a real conversation with them in over a year.
Host: [honestly] Does that illusion cause problems when people are eventually confronted with the real distance between them?
Guest: Frequently. We interviewed people who were genuinely shocked to realize a 'close' friend hadn't been told about a major life event, simply because nobody had actually spoken in months.
Host: [gently] What would you say separates a friendship that survives distance from one that quietly dissolves despite frequent digital contact?
Guest: Reciprocity, mainly. If only one person is consistently the one initiating deeper conversations, the relationship is being sustained by effort rather than mutual investment.
Host: [calmly] Can that imbalance be corrected, or is it usually too late by the time someone notices?
Guest: It can be corrected, provided both people are willing to name the imbalance honestly, rather than letting resentment build silently underneath the surface.
Host: [encouraging] Any practical advice for listeners who suspect they're the only one making an effort?
Guest: Test it, gently. Step back briefly, not as punishment, but simply to observe whether the other person notices your absence at all.
Guest: Then you likely already have your answer, even if it's not the one you were hoping for.
Host: That's a sobering thought, but an important one. Thank you, Teguh, for such a candid conversation.
Guest: My pleasure. I hope it gives listeners something worth reflecting on.

quiz.question: What does Teguh's research find about constant low-effort digital contact?
options: It can substitute for the deeper conversations that used to sustain friendships
It always strengthens friendships equally
It has no effect on relationships at all
It only matters for family relationships
quiz.explanation: Teguh explains that constant low-effort contact can substitute for the deeper conversations that used to sustain friendships.

quiz.question: What surprised the people interviewed in Teguh's research?
options: A 'close' friend hadn't been told about a major life event because nobody had actually spoken in months
Their friends remembered every detail of their lives
They had too many close friends
Digital contact was more meaningful than expected
quiz.explanation: Interviewees were shocked that a close friend hadn't been told about a major life event, since nobody had actually spoken in months.

quiz.question: What does Teguh say mainly separates surviving friendships from dissolving ones?
options: How often they post online
Living in the same city
Having identical schedules
Reciprocity, meaning both people initiate deeper conversations rather than just one
quiz.explanation: Teguh says reciprocity is the main factor; if only one person initiates, the relationship is sustained by effort rather than mutual investment.

quiz.question: What does Teguh suggest testing if you suspect you're the only one making an effort?
options: Confronting the friend angrily
Ending the friendship immediately
Asking mutual friends to intervene
Stepping back briefly to observe whether the other person notices your absence
quiz.explanation: Teguh suggests gently stepping back, not as punishment, to observe whether the other person notices your absence at all.

quiz.question: According to Teguh, what does it mean if the other person doesn't notice your absence?
options: It means nothing significant
It means you should message them more often
It proves they are simply very busy
You likely already have your answer about the friendship
quiz.explanation: Teguh says that if they don't notice, you likely already have your answer, even if it's not the one you hoped for.

quiz.question: How can constant online reactions create a false sense of closeness?
options: I never applied for this role, exactly
I offered to help last week and he practically refused
They replace deeper conversations while preserving an appearance of contact.
Rian began calling not because he was in crisis
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: They replace deeper conversations while preserving an appearance of contact.

quiz.question: What discovery shocked participants in the sociologist's research?
options: I realized then that mediating hadn't made me impartial
A supposed close friend had missed a major life event.
People accept help far more easily when it doesn't feel entirely one-directional
What began as a favor to my aunt became, unexpectedly, one of the relationships I value most
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: A supposed close friend had missed a major life event.

quiz.question: Which feature helps a friendship survive distance?
options: That announcement did not go over well
Let's visit him this evening, then
Both people initiate meaningful contact and invest in the relationship.
I used to think mentoring meant having answers
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: Both people initiate meaningful contact and invest in the relationship.

quiz.question: How can friends repair an imbalance before resentment grows?
options: I still care deeply about their marriage
They can name the unequal effort honestly and change it together.
If we get this right, he might actually enjoy the arrangement more than he lets on
He cried, a little
quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: They can name the unequal effort honestly and change it together.

quiz.question: What gentle test does Teguh suggest for a one-sided friendship?
options: These days, when they call to complain about each other, I still listen
Step back briefly and see whether the other person notices.
Most people do, honestly, regardless of how old they happen to be

quiz.explanation: This matches the audio: Step back briefly and see whether the other person notices.
